blocks.text: Basic Pointers:
'e Judiciary in India is Integrated (borrowed from Gol act of 1935) and Independent.
The Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court and the Judicial Committee of Privy Council after India gained Independence.
1st sitting: 28 Jan, 1950
Federal Court was established in 1937 under the provisions of Gol Act 1935.
SC is also known as 'the Guardian of the Constitution.' PART V -SUPREME COURT Chapter I'V: [Article 124-147]
Article 124: Establishment and Constitution of Supreme Court 124(1) Strength of Judges
Originally, strength: 1 Chief Justice + 7 Judges = 8 Judges
Present, strength: 1 Chief Justice + 33 Judges = 34 Judges (Maximum sanctioned strength: 34)
124(2) Every judge of SC shall be appointed by the President after consultation with CJI (Collegium).

The Sapru Committee (1944-45), chaired by Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, recommended the establishment of an independent judiciary including a Supreme Court; however, the provisions relating to the appointment of judges in the Indian Constitution were not solely based on its recommendations but evolved through multiple constitutional sources and debates.
Collegium System (Not mentioned in Constitution)

It is a system under which appointments and transfers of judges are decided by a forum of the CJI and the 4 senior most judges of the Supreme Court. It has no place in the Indian constitution. Its origin can be traced from the following judges cases:
First Judges Case (1982 - S.P. Gupta Case):
Recommendation of CJI not binding on the President.
Gave primacy to the executive in judicial appointments.
Second Judges Case (1993):
Introduced the Collegium system, holding that "Consultation" means Concurrence.
Recommendation made by CJI + 2 senior-most judges will be binding on President.
Third Judges Case (1998):
Collegium expanded to a 5 member body,

CJI + 4 senior-most judges, recommendation binding on the President. 3 The Parliament replaced the collegium system by National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) through 99th CA, 2014 to provide recommendations to the President.
Fourth Judges Case (SC Advocate on record association case - 2015):
99th CA was declared unconstitutional and NJAC Act was struck down.
Collegium System was restored.
Tenure: Serves till the age of 65 years, provided that— (a) A Judge may resign his office by writing to the President.
(b) A Judge to be removed in the manner provided in clause 124(2A) The age of a SC Judge to be determined in such manner as Parliament may by law provide. (15th CAA, 1963)
124(3) Qualification for SC Judges:
(a) A Citizen of India.
(b) At least 5 years as a Judge of a High Court, or — (c) At least 10 years as an Advocate of a High Court, or — (d) Distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President.
(e) No minimum Age for Appointment is Mentioned.

124(4) Removal (Borrowed from U.S.A): A Judge can be removed by President after Parliament passes an address by Special Majority (i.e. majority of total membership + 2/3rd of members present and voting) on grounds of:
Proved misbehaviour or Incapacity
Procedure of Removal for Supreme Court/High Court Judges is mentioned in Judges Enquiry Act, 1968
Motion to remove judges should be signed by 50 members of Rajya Sabha or 100 members of Lok Sabha.
Justice V. Ramaswami was the first Supreme Court judge to face impeachment proceedings, with a motion initiated against him in 1991.
124(5)Parliament may by law establish procedure for investi- gating judge's misconduct as mentioned in clause (4).
124(6) A Judge of SC to subscribe an Oath or affirmation before the President.
124(7) Restrictions: After retirement, a SC judge cannot practice law in any court within the territory of India.
Article 125: Salaries, etc., of Judges
Salaries & allowances are determined by Parliament Article 126: Appointment of Acting Chief Justice President appoints Acting Chief Justice when:
Chief Justice's seat is vacant, or
Chief Justice is unable to perform his duties.
First Female Judge of SC: Justice Fathima Beevi (1989)
No Female Chief Justice of SC till date.
B.V Nagarathana is expected to become the 1st woman _ Chief Justice of India in September 2027 on the basis of Article 127: Appointment of Ad Hoc Judges
CJL, with prior consent of the President and in consultation with the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court, may request a High Court judge (qualified for SC)
to sit as an ad hoc judge (temporary judge) in the Supreme Court.
Such ad hoc judge enjoys powers, jurisdiction, and privileges of SC judges during the time.
Article 128; Attendance of Retired Judges
Retired SC Judges can be invited to sit and act as Judge of Article 129: Supreme Court is a Court of Record which means:
Its decisions are preserved as legal precedents.
It has power to punish for 'Contempt of court.' (Nowhere defined in Constitution)
Article 130: Seat of Supreme Court
The seat of the Supreme Court is at Delhi.
SC can sit elsewhere if CJI recommends and President approves.
Article 131: Original Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
SC has Exclusive Original Jurisdiction in disputes:
Between Government of India and one or more States.
Between Gol and any state or states on one side and one or more states on the other side.
Between two or more States.
Article 131 (A): introduced by 42nd CA, 1976. It granted SC exclusive authority to determine the validity of central laws, it was further repealed by 43rd CA, 1977.
Further this jurisdiction of SC does not extend to following matters:
Dispute arising out of Pre-Constitutional Treaties.
Inter-State water Disputes.
Matter related to Finance Commission.
Article 132: Appellate Jurisdiction of SC (Constitutional Matters)
By way of appeal from HC to the SC of India in Constitutional matters.
Article 133: Appellate Jurisdiction of SC (Civil Matters)
Appeal to SC from HC on judgments in civil cases like:
Property, Marriage, Divorce, etc.
Article 134: Appellate Jurisdiction (Criminal Matters)
Article 135: Federal Court's Powers
SC can exercise powers of the Federal Court under pre-Constitution laws.
Article 136: Special Leave to Appeal
SC can grant Special Leave to appeal from any court/ tribunal judgment (except those related to Armed forces courts or Military Tribunals/Court-Martial.)
Article 137: Review of Judgments
SC can review its own judgments or orders.
Justice Syed Shah Mohammed Quadri classified Judicial · Review into the following three categories:

1. Judicial review of constitutional amendments 2. Judicial review of legislation of the Parliament and State Legislatures and subordinate legislations 3. Judicial review of administrative action of the Union and States and authorities under the state.
Judicial review borrowed from the U.S. Constitution.
Article 138: Enlargement of SC Jurisdiction
Parliament may expand SC's jurisdiction by law.
Article 139: Power to Issue Certain Writs
SC can issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights given under Article 32.
For other purposes, it requires Parliamentary permission.

139A Empowers the Supreme Court to transfer cases, appeals, or proceedings from one or more High Courts to itself Article 140: Ancillary (Supportive) Powers of Supreme Court Article 141: Law Declared by SC to be binding on all Courts Article 141 Article 142 Article 142: Enforcement of Decrees and Orders
SC may pass any decree/ order for doing complete justice in any matter.
Judicial Activism: Is a powerful tool that enables the SC to go beyond strict laws to ensure fairness. Eg.- 1. Union carbide cooperation vs Union of India case - 1989.
2. Vishakha vs State of Rajasthan (1997) - Guidelines Dealing with sexual harassment of women at workplace.
3. Ayodhya Verdict (2019) - Land allocation for complete Justice.
Article 143: Advisory Jurisdiction
President may refer 2 kinds of matters to SC for advice.
1. Pre-constitutional matters
2. Matters of General importance
In pre-constitutional matters, SC must give its advice to President, and in both the cases, the advice is not binding on him/her.
Article 144: Civil and Judicial Authorities to Act in Aid of SC Article 145: Rules of Court, etc.
SC can make its own procedural rules with President's approval as long as it does not conflict with the laws made by the Parliament.
Article 146: Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court.
Appointments: CJI of SC appoints the Court's officers and Staff.
Service Conditions: CJI sets the rules for the staff employment and salaries.
Expenses: The SC operating cost, like staff salaries, pensions are paid from Consolidated Fund of India.
Article 147: Interpretation Constitution clarifies that when interpreting the constitution, any significant legal question should also be considered:
GOI Act, 1935, Indian Independence Act, 1947 and related orders and amendments to both of these Acts.

Article 214: Establishment of High Courts
Each State shall have a High Court.
At Present - 25 High Courts.
Article 215: High Court to be Court of Record Article 216: Constitution of High Courts
One Chief Justice and other Judges as President may decide.

Article 217: Appointment and Conditions of Judges 217(1) Appointment of HC Judges is done by the President after consultation with: Chief Justice of India, Governor of State, Chief Justice of the High Court. (Collegium)
Maximum age for HC Judge: 62 years
HC judge shall hand his resignation to the President.
His Removal process is same as that of SC Judge.
217(2) Qualifications: 10 years advocate of HC, or
10 years holding judicial office.
217(3) Inserted by the 15th Amendment (1963), this provision ensures the President's decision is final and not subject to judicial review.
No provision for "Distinguished Jurist" in HC.
Article 218; Application of Certain Provisions i pee
Applies SC Judges' removal procedure to HC Judges, Judges Inquiry Act, 1968.
Article 219: Oath or Affirmation
HC judge take oath before the Governor.
Article 220: Restriction on Practice After Retirement
Former HC judges cannot practice law before any court except: SC & other HCs.
Article 221: Salaries and Allowances
Salaries and allowances are drawn from Consolidated Fund of State while Pensions are drawn from Consolidated Fund of India.
Salaries, allowances, leaves and pension rights are determined by the Parliament.
Article 222: Transfer of Judges
President can transfer HC judges after consultation with Article 223: Appointment of Acting Chief Justice
The President can appoint an Acting Chief Justice when:
(a) The office of the Chief Justice of the High Court is vacant, or (b) The Chief Justice is unable to perform duties due to absence or any other reason.

Article 224: Appointment of Additional and Acting Judges 1. Additional Judges: If the workload of High Court increases (e.g. due to arrears), the President may appoint additional judges for a temporary period not exceeding 2 years.
2. Acting Judges: If a judge is absent, unable to perform duties, or seat is vacant, the President may appoint an acting judge.
These appointments to be done in consultation with CJI.
Article 224A: Appointment of Retired Judges at Sittings of High Courts
The Chief Justice of a HC can request the attendance of a retired judge of that HC or any other HC.
Article 225: Jurisdiction of HC
Original jurisdiction - revenue matters, election disputes of MPs and MLAs.
Appellate jurisdiction - hear appeals about decisions made by lower courts.
Article 226: Power of HC to Issue Writs
HC has wider writ jurisdiction than SC
It can issue writs on Legal + Fundamental Rights.
HC may refuse to issue writ, SC cannot.
Article 227: Superintendence over Subordinate Courts They also manage appeals from subordinate courts and have administrative control over the district judiciary.
Article 228: Transfer of Certain Cases to HC Article 229: Officers and Servants of HC - by Chief Justice of HC.
Article 230: Extension of Jurisdiction to Union Territories:
Power of Parliament —
Andaman & Nicobar > Calcutta HC
Lakshadweep > Kerala HC
Puducherry > Madras HC
Dadra and Nagar Haveli & Daman and Diu > Maharashtra HC.
Chandigarh > Punjab and Haryana HC

Article 231: Establishment of Common High Court for two or more States. (7th CA, 1956) for example: a. Maharashtra and Goa have a common HC at Mumbai, Maharashtra. b. Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram and Assam have a common HC at Guwahati, Assam.
Article 232: Transfer of Cases to Federal Court (Repealed)
By the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.
1st HC (1862): Calcutta High Court.
1st Female HC Judge: Justice Anna Chandy - Appointed to Kerala High Court.
1st Female Chief Justice of HC: Justice Leila Seth of Himachal Pradesh High Court TRICK - NHRC AAO ReST karo (for Article 214-222)

233(2): A person not already in the service of the Union or of the State shall only be eligible to be appointed a district judge if he has been for not less than seven years an advocate or a pleader and is recommended by the High Court for appointment.
Judicial Review is done by High Court.
233(3): A District Judge in India holds the highest judicial authority in a district, exercising both original and appellate civil jurisdiction.

Article 233A: The 20th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1966 inserted Article 233A in the Constitution of India to validate irregular appointments, postings, and promotions of district judges, ensuring the legality of their judgments.
Article 234: Recruitment of Persons Other than District Judges to the Judicial Services shall be made by the Governor of the state.
Article 235: Control Over Subordinate Courts.

A sentence of death (capital punishment) passed by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge requires mandatory confirmation by the High Court under Section 366 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973.
Article 237: The Governor can extend judicial service rules to certain magistrates under Article 237 of the Constitution of India.
Article 241; Separate High Court can be created for UTs.
Criminal appeals are heard by the Court of Session, and civil appeals by the District Court.
The Family Courts Act, 1984

The Family Courts Act, 1984 (Act No. 66 of 1984) was enacted in India on September 14, 1984, to establish specialized Family Courts for promoting conciliation and securing speedy settlements in disputes relating to marriage and family affairs, for cities with populations over one million.
Appeals against the orders of the Family Court lie to the High Court and must be heard by a bench of two or more judges.
These courts handle cases like simple money claims, small rent disputes, and contractual matters.
The decrees and orders are generally final but subject to High Court's revision.
Governed by the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887.
It is one of the alternative dispute redressal mechanisms.
Established under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, to settle pending or pre-litigation disputes amicably.
It came into force on 9th November 1995
Inspiration drawn from Ancient Indian Dispute Resolution.
No court fee is required to bring a case to Lok Adalat.
The award is final, binding, and cannot be appealed.
Divorce and non-compoundable offenses cannot be dealt by Lok Adalats.
The permanent Lok Adalat can handle cases up to a certain monetary limit (currently Rs. 1 cr).
There is no court fee and if court fee is already paid, the amount will be refunded if the dispute is settled at Lok Adalat.
The award by the Lok Adalat is binding on the parties and it has the status of a decree of a civil court and it is non- appealable.
Public Interest Litigation
It is a legal mechanism in India, introduced in the 1980s by justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna lyer.
It relaxes the rule of locus standi.
Locus Standi: It is a Latin term meaning "the right to be heard" or "the right to approach the court."
Any public-spirited person can file a case even if they are not directly affected.

S.P. Gupta vs. Union of India (1981) - The landmark judgment marked the beginning of liberalisation of the doctrine of locus standi and laid the foundation for Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India.
To provide access to justice for the poor, downtrodden, and illiterate, and to ensure accountability of public authorities.
PILs can be filed directly in the Supreme Court of India (under Article 32) or High Courts (under Article 226).
Added by 42nd CAA,1976.
Tribunals are quasi-Judicial bodies.
Key Constitutional Provisions (Part XIV-A)
Article 323A (Administrative Tribunals): Empowers Parliament to set up tribunals for adjudication of disputes related to recruitment and service conditions of public servants.

Article 323B (Tribunals for Other Matters): Empowers Parliament and State Legislatures to create tribunals for spe- cific subjects, including taxation, foreign exchange, industrial / labor disputes, land reforms, elections, and rent/tenancy.

In L. Chandra Kumar case (1997) SC held that tribunals established under Articles 323A/323B are not substitutes for High Courts and are subject to their jurisdiction & hence their decisions are subject to Judicial Review Some important facts to know:
Before being elevated to the Supreme Court of India and subsequently appointed as the 52nd Chief Justice of India, Justice B.R. Gavai served as a Judge of the Bombay High Court.
The Court of Munsiff (or Munsif Court), also known as the Civil Judge (Junior Division) court, is the primary judicial body in India that handles civil cases with small pecuniary stakes.
The High Court of Delhi continued to exercise jurisdiction over the Union Territory of Himachal Pradesh until January

The concept of a Curative Petition was introduced by the Supreme Court of India in the landmark case of Rupa Ashok Hurra V. Ashok Hurra 2002. It was established as a final legal remedy to prevent gross miscarriages of justice, allowing the Court to reconsider a judgment even after a review petition
The term 'Judicial Activism' was first coined by: Arthur Schlesinger Jr.
